title: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
summary: How an SSD hides erase-before-write NAND flash behind a block interface: the log-structured FTL, garbage collection and write amplification math, over-provisioning, TRIM, wear, and NVMe queues.
outcomes: Explain why NAND flash cannot overwrite a page in place and why a direct-mapped layout is slow and wears blocks out
Trace a page-mapped log-structured FTL through writes, overwrites and garbage collection, and size its mapping table
Compute write amplification from victim utilization and estimate it from spare factor for random writes
Choose levers that lower write amplification: over-provisioning, TRIM, sequential writes, hot/cold separation, FDP
Describe NVMe submission and completion queues, doorbells and phase tags, and size queue depth with Little's law

lessons.title: Why flash cannot overwrite a page in place

blocks.md:
Recall from OS basics that a disk is a **block device**: the OS reads and writes fixed-size sectors by number, the *logical block address* (LBA). A hard disk can rewrite sector 7 by simply writing over it. An SSD offers exactly the same interface, but the chips inside it cannot do that. This course explains what the drive does instead and why that costs throughput and lifetime.

An SSD stores bits in **NAND flash**. Each cell traps electric charge; a single-level cell (SLC) stores 1 bit, multi-level (MLC) 2 bits and triple-level (TLC) 3 bits per cell. More bits per cell means cheaper capacity but slower, less durable cells.

Flash is organized in two units of different size:

- A **page** (a few KB, for example 4 KB) is the unit of reading and writing.
- An **erase block** (OSTEP gives 128 KB to 2 MB) holds many pages and is the unit of erasing.

The Samsung part studied by Agrawal et al. has 4 KB pages, 64 pages per block (256 KB), 2048 blocks per plane and 4 planes per die. Note the clash of words: a flash *block* is not a file system block and a flash *page* is not a virtual memory page.

A flash chip supports only three operations:

1. **Read** a page: tens of microseconds (25 us on the Samsung SLC part).
2. **Program** a page: can only change bits from 1 to 0, and only on a page that was erased. 200 us on that part.
3. **Erase** a whole block: sets every bit in it back to 1. 1.5 ms on that part.

OSTEP's table shows reads, programs and erases all get slower as you pack more bits per cell (TLC programs take roughly 900 to 1350 us, erases about 4.5 ms). Pages inside a block must also be programmed in order, low to high, to limit disturbance of neighboring cells.

blocks.title: Overwriting one page of a 4-page block

scenes.caption: OSTEP's toy block: four 8-bit pages, all programmed (shown in hex: 0x18 is 00011000). We want page 0 to hold 0x03 (00000011).
Programming can only turn 1s into 0s. Going from 00011000 to 00000011 needs two bits to become 1, so the page cannot be reprogrammed directly.
The only way to get 1s back is to erase the whole block. Every page becomes 0xFF (all ones) and ERASED, including pages 1 to 3 we wanted to keep.
Now page 0 can be programmed with 0x03. Its neighbours' old contents are gone unless something copied them away before the erase.

blocks.md: Flash is **write once per erase**: a page can be programmed once, and the only reset is erasing an entire block of many pages. Everything clever inside an SSD exists to hide this asymmetry from the block interface above it.

Flash also **wears out**. Each program/erase (P/E) cycle leaves a little trapped charge behind until 0 and 1 can no longer be told apart. OSTEP reports manufacturers rating MLC blocks at about 10,000 P/E cycles and SLC at about 100,000, while noting measurements that found real endurance can be much higher. Either way it is finite, so a block that gets erased much more often than its neighbours dies first.

The obvious design, a **direct-mapped** layer, keeps logical page N at physical page N. To overwrite one 4 KB page it must read the other 63 live pages of the 256 KB block, erase the block, then program all 64 pages back. One host write becomes 64 page programs, and the same physical block is erased every time the host rewrites a hot address.

blocks.title: Time for one 4 KB overwrite (Samsung SLC timings)

scenes.caption: Direct-mapped: read 63 pages (63 x 25 us), erase the block (1500 us), program 64 pages (64 x 200 us). Total 15,875 us. Simplified: ignores the 100 us per page bus transfer.
Writing to an already-erased page elsewhere: one 200 us program, plus one 1500 us erase shared by the 64 pages of a block (23.4 us each). Total 223.4 us, about 71x faster.

blocks.prompt: Given these costs, what should the drive do when the host overwrites logical page 7?
blocks.reveal: Never overwrite in place. Write the new data to a fresh, already-erased page somewhere else, remember that logical page 7 now lives there, and mark the old copy as stale. The erase is postponed and shared by many writes. That is the idea of the next lesson: a log-structured flash translation layer.

blocks.question: A drive uses a direct-mapped layout with 256 KB erase blocks of 4 KB pages. The host overwrites a single 4 KB page. How many page programs does the flash perform?
options: 1, because only one page changed
63, the other live pages
64, the whole block is rewritten after the erase
128, one read and one program per page
blocks.explain: After erasing, every page of the block is blank, so all 64 pages (63 preserved plus the new one) must be programmed. That is 64x more flash writing than the host asked for, and the block takes one more P/E cycle per host write.

blocks.question: The drive wants page 0 to go from 0x18 (00011000) to 0x03 (00000011) without an erase. Why is that impossible?
options: A program takes longer than an erase
Programming can only turn 1 bits into 0 bits, and 0x03 needs two 0 bits to become 1
The page must first be copied into DRAM
Only the last page of a block can be programmed
blocks.explain: Programming only clears bits (1 to 0). Setting bits back to 1 takes a block erase. In practice FTLs never reprogram a programmed page at all: OSTEP's state diagram treats a second program of the same page as an error.

lessons.title: The flash translation layer: a log plus a map

blocks.md: Inside an SSD sit several flash packages, a controller running firmware, and some DRAM or SRAM. The firmware layer that turns block reads and writes into flash reads, programs and erases is the **flash translation layer (FTL)**. Its goals: high performance, low **write amplification** (flash bytes written divided by host bytes written) and even wear across blocks.

blocks.title: Where an I/O goes inside an SSD

scenes.caption: The host only sees logical block addresses. The controller owns the flash and keeps a table mapping each logical page to a physical page.
A read: the controller looks up the LBA in the mapping table, then reads that physical page from whichever package holds it.
A write: the controller picks the next erased page in its current write block, programs it, and updates the table. Multiple packages let it work on several writes at once.

blocks.md: Most FTLs are **log structured**: every write is appended to the next free page of the block currently being filled, whatever its logical address, and the mapping table records where each logical page now lives. Overwriting a logical page leaves its old physical copy behind as **garbage** (also called stale or dead). Let us replay OSTEP's example: 3 blocks of 4 pages, and writes to logical addresses 100, 101, 2000, 2001.

blocks.title: A page-mapped log-structured FTL, step by step

scenes.caption: Pages 0 to 11 form blocks 0, 1 and 2 (4 pages each). All start invalid (i): nothing is erased yet. The map is empty.
Write(100, a1). The FTL erases block 0 (E), programs page 0, and records 100 to page 0 in the map.
Writes to 101, 2000 and 2001 go to the next free pages 1, 2, 3, in order. Random logical addresses became one sequential physical stream.
Overwrite 100 and 101 with c1, c2. The FTL erases block 1 and appends to pages 4 and 5; the map moves. Pages 0 and 1 still hold a1, a2 but nothing points to them: garbage.
Garbage collection on block 0: copy its live pages (b1, b2) to the end of the log (pages 6, 7), update the map, then erase block 0. Two extra page writes were spent to free 4 pages.

blocks.md: How does the GC know page 2 is live? Each page stores the logical address it holds in a small out-of-band (OOB) area. The collector checks the map: if the map still points at this page, it is live. The same OOB data lets the drive rebuild the map after power loss by scanning, which is slow, so higher-end drives also checkpoint the map.
The second cost of page mapping is the table itself. One entry per 4 KB page, 4 bytes per entry:

blocks.caption: Mapping table for a 1 TiB drive with 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries (OSTEP's example).

blocks.md:
Three ways around that memory bill, all described in OSTEP:

- **Block mapping**: one entry per 256 KB block, 64x smaller (16 MiB for 1 TiB). But a 4 KB write must copy the whole block's other pages, the direct-mapped problem again.
- **Hybrid mapping**: most data is block-mapped, while a few *log blocks* are page-mapped and absorb new writes. Log blocks are later merged back: a cheap *switch merge* if a whole block was rewritten in order, a *partial merge* if some pages must be copied, and an expensive *full merge* gathering pages from many blocks.
- **Page mapping plus caching** (DFTL): keep the full page map on flash and cache the hot part in RAM. Works well with locality; a miss costs an extra flash read.

blocks.question: A block-mapped FTL stores logical pages 2000 to 2003 in one 4-page physical block. The host overwrites only 2002. How many pages must be programmed?
blocks.explain: With one pointer per block, the block's pages must stay together in order. The FTL reads 2000, 2001 and 2003, then writes all four (with the new 2002) into a fresh block. With real 64-page blocks that is 64 programs for one host page.

blocks.question: In the log-structured example, right after logical 100 and 101 are overwritten, why can't the FTL reuse physical pages 0 and 1 immediately?
options: They are still referenced by the map
Erasing works on whole blocks, and block 0 still holds live pages 2 and 3
Pages can only be reused after a power cycle
The FTL must wait for the host to send TRIM
blocks.explain: Pages 0 and 1 are dead, but the only way to make them writable is erasing block 0, which would destroy b1 and b2. Those live pages must be copied out first: that copy is garbage collection, and it is where write amplification comes from.

lessons.title: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula

blocks.md: The FTL needs a steady supply of erased blocks. When free blocks run low, the garbage collector (also called the cleaner) picks a **victim** block, copies its still-valid pages to the write frontier, and erases it. The copies are writes the host never asked for. **Write amplification** $A$ is total flash writes divided by host writes, so $A = 1$ means no extra writes.

Suppose every victim has a fraction $u$ of its $N_p$ pages still valid. Cleaning it copies $u N_p$ pages and gains $(1-u) N_p$ free pages, which the host then fills. So for every $(1-u) N_p$ host pages the flash programs $N_p$ pages in total:

blocks.caption: Steady state: write amplification depends only on how full the victim blocks are when they are cleaned.

x.label: u: valid fraction of the victim block

scenes.caption: Empty victims (u = 0) are free to clean: A = 1. A victim with 48 of 64 pages valid (u = 0.75) costs 48 copies to free 16 pages: A = 4.
The curve explodes near u = 1. At u = 0.9 the drive writes 10 pages of flash per host page; at 0.95 it writes 20.
Everything that lowers u at cleaning time lowers A: spare capacity, smart victim choice, TRIM and grouping data that dies together.

blocks.md:
Two classic victim policies:

- **FIFO / LRU cleaning**: clean the oldest-written block. Simple, but it may pick a block that is still mostly valid.
- **Greedy cleaning**: clean the block with the fewest valid pages. Agrawal et al. use a greedy cleaner; Desnoyers notes greedy has been proven optimal for uniform random traffic.

Both are bounded by how much free space exists. If the user can fill the whole drive with live data, garbage only exists in the spare area the user cannot see.

That hidden spare is **over-provisioning**. Desnoyers defines the **spare factor** $S_f = (T-U)/T$ for $T$ physical and $U$ logical blocks. For uniformly random 4 KB overwrites and FIFO cleaning, Desnoyers derives an exact model: a page survives its trip through the queue with probability $e^{-\alpha/A}$ where $\alpha = T/U$, which gives

blocks.caption: W is the Lambert W function (inverse of x e^x). Equivalently u solves u = exp(-alpha (1-u)) and A = 1/(1-u).

blocks.prompt: A drive has 7% spare (S_f = 0.07) and the host overwrites random 4 KB pages across its whole capacity forever. Roughly what write amplification do you expect?
blocks.reveal: About **7.3** with FIFO cleaning (the formula gives 7.318, matching Desnoyers' simulation) and about **6.6** with greedy cleaning (Desnoyers' Table 2: 6.623; our own 64-page simulation got 6.65). Victims are still about 86% valid when cleaned, because random overwrites spread garbage thinly over every block. Seven percent spare does not mean seven percent overhead.

blocks.title: Uniform random writes: write amplification versus spare

scenes.caption: FIFO cleaning, from the closed-form model: 10.17, 5.18, 2.69, 1.99. Doubling spare from 5% to 10% halves the extra writing.
Greedy cleaning, our simulation (64-page blocks, 192,000 logical pages): 8.91, 4.84, 2.60, 1.94. Better than FIFO, most of all at low spare. Simplified: ignores wear leveling and erase time.

blocks.title: One greedy cleaning step
blocks.code:
Np = 4
valid = [3, 1, 4, 2]          # live pages per sealed block
victim = valid.index(min(valid))
copies = valid[victim]
freed = Np - copies
flash_writes = Np             # copies + host pages that refill it
host_writes = freed
A = flash_writes / host_writes

scenes.caption: Four sealed blocks of 4 pages hold 3, 1, 4 and 2 live pages.
Greedy picks the block with the fewest live pages: block 1.
One live page must be copied out before the erase, which frees 3 pages for new host data.
Over this cycle the flash programs 4 pages for 3 host pages: A = 4/3, about 1.33. A cleaner that picked block 2 (4 live) would free nothing at all.

blocks.md: Access pattern matters as much as spare. A large **sequential** write fills whole blocks with data that is later overwritten or deleted together, so victims come back almost empty and $A$ stays near 1. In Agrawal et al.'s simulated SSD with cleaning enabled, sequential writes ran at 24,457 IO/s (327 us) and random writes at 18,480 IO/s (433 us), and random-write cost grows with how little locality the workload has.

A drive does not know which LBAs your file system considers free. Unless told (lesson 4), every LBA ever written counts as live. Agrawal et al. put it bluntly: unlike a log-structured file system, the disk here is always full, so cleaning pressure is maximal all the time.

blocks.question: A greedy cleaner finds that the best victim has 60 of its 64 pages valid. What is the write amplification of this cleaning cycle?
options: About 1.07
blocks.explain: It copies 60 pages to free 4. The flash writes 64 pages (60 copies plus 4 host pages) for 4 host pages: 64/4 = 16. This is what happens on a nearly full drive under random writes.

blocks.question: Two drives have identical flash. Drive X exposes 960 GB from 1024 GB of flash, drive Y exposes 1000 GB. Under sustained random overwrites, which is true?
options: Same write amplification, since the flash is identical
Y has lower write amplification because it has more capacity to spread writes
X has higher amplification because GC runs more often
X has lower write amplification because more spare means emptier victims
blocks.explain: X has S_f = 64/1024, about 6.3%; Y has 24/1024, about 2.3%. Less spare means victims are fuller when cleaned, and A = 1/(1-u) rises steeply as u approaches 1.

lessons.title: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance

blocks.md: Log structuring already spreads writes: each new write lands in a freshly erased block, wherever it is. But a block full of **cold data** (written once, never overwritten) is never chosen by the cleaner, so it stops aging while the hot blocks absorb all the erases. **Wear leveling** fixes this by periodically moving cold data out of rarely erased blocks so those blocks rejoin the rotation. The moves are extra writes: wear leveling trades a little write amplification for even wear.

blocks.title: Agrawal et al.: wear after an IOzone run

scenes.caption: Standard deviation of remaining block lifetime (in cycles, lifetime cut to 50 for the experiment). Mean lifetime was about 43 to 44 in all three; only migrating cold data tightened the spread (13.47 to 5.71).
Blocks that exceeded the erase limit: 223 with plain greedy, 153 with rate limiting of worn blocks, 0 with cold-data migration. The migrations added a 4.7% latency overhead.

blocks.md: **TRIM** is the host telling the drive which logical blocks it no longer needs. The FTL can drop their mappings and treat their pages as garbage, so they are never copied during cleaning. In NVMe this is the Dataset Management command with the deallocate attribute; on Linux, `fstrim` discards all unused blocks of a mounted file system, and its man page says once a week is sufficient for most systems (the `discard` mount option trims continuously instead).

blocks.prompt: A drive has 7% spare. The file system keeps only half of the logical space in use and trims the rest, and overwrites are uniformly random over the live half. What happens to write amplification under the FIFO model?
blocks.reveal: The trimmed half acts as extra spare. Live data is 0.5 x 0.93 = 46.5% of the flash, so the effective spare factor is 0.535 and the model gives A of about **1.20**, versus **7.32** when all LBAs are live. Agrawal et al. make the same point: a half-full disk has twice the cleaning efficiency of a full one, and every disk is full unless it is told otherwise.

blocks.md: Real workloads are skewed: in some Microsoft Research traces Desnoyers examined, half the writes hit 1% or less of the address space. Mixing hot pages (rewritten often) and cold pages in the same blocks is wasteful: when a block is cleaned, its cold pages are still valid and get copied again and again. **Hot/cold separation** writes the two kinds into different blocks, so hot blocks die almost completely and cold blocks rarely need cleaning. Desnoyers shows that for the paper's hot/cold traffic model, separation removes the loss caused by non-uniform traffic.

blocks.title: Skewed writes with 10% spare and greedy cleaning

scenes.caption: Our simulation (64-page blocks): uniform random writes give A = 4.84. With 80% of writes to 20% of pages and hot and cold pages mixed in one write stream, greedy gives 5.16 (Desnoyers' model: 5.17). Skew made it worse.

Separate write frontiers for hot and cold pages with plain greedy cleaning give 4.85, back to the uniform value: each pool acts like its own uniform FTL with the same spare fraction. Separation removes the loss but gains nothing yet.

The gain comes from giving the hot pool a larger share of the spare. Desnoyers' example, 90% of writes to 5% of pages: uniform 4.82, mixed greedy 6.24, separation with the optimal split of free space 1.86.

blocks.md: The drive cannot always guess which data dies together, but the host often knows (a log file, a compaction output, a cache). NVMe 2.x adds **Flexible Data Placement (FDP)**: the host tags each write with a placement identifier that selects a *reclaim unit*, a region the controller can erase without disturbing others. The spec states the goal directly: let the host reduce write amplification by aligning data to the media. Its FDP Statistics log reports host bytes written and media bytes written, whose ratio is exactly the measured write amplification.
Endurance is where write amplification turns into money. If every block survives $E$ P/E cycles and the drive has capacity $C$, the host can write roughly

blocks.caption: Simplified: ignores spare area, uneven wear and the fact that real endurance differs from the rating.

blocks.title: Lifetime host writes for a 1 TB drive

scenes.caption: With OSTEP's 10,000-cycle MLC rating, a 1 TB drive could absorb 10 PB of host writes at A = 1 but only 2.5 PB at A = 4.
Lower-endurance cells shrink everything proportionally. At 3,000 cycles and A = 4, the same drive is rated for 0.75 PB.

blocks.md: You can watch this on a real drive. The NVMe SMART / Health log reports **Data Units Written** in thousands of 512-byte units (a value of 2,000,000 means about 2,000,000 x 1000 x 512 B = 1.024 TB written by the host) and **Percentage Used**, a vendor estimate of life consumed that is allowed to exceed 100. Data Units Written counts host writes only; the extra writes from garbage collection are not included.

Lifetime and throughput both scale with 1/A. The levers to lower A are all about making victim blocks emptier: more spare, TRIM of dead data, writes that are large and sequential, and grouping data that will die at the same time.

blocks.question: A service writes 300 TB per year to a 1 TB drive rated for 10,000 P/E cycles. The drive's FDP statistics show media bytes written are 5x host bytes. Roughly how long until rated wear-out?
options: About 6.7 years
About 33 years
About 1.3 years
Never, wear leveling prevents it
blocks.explain: Lifetime host writes = 1 TB x 10,000 / 5 = 2,000 TB. At 300 TB per year that is 2000/300, about 6.7 years. Halving A to 2.5 would double it.

blocks.question: A database deletes old SSTable files but the file system is mounted without discard and fstrim never runs. What happens inside the SSD?
options: Nothing changes: deleted files free their flash pages automatically
The FTL still considers those LBAs live, so cleaning keeps copying dead data and write amplification rises
The drive becomes read-only
The data is erased immediately to free space
blocks.explain: Deleting a file only updates file system metadata. Until the LBAs are trimmed (deallocated), the drive must preserve their contents and copies them during every cleaning of their blocks.

lessons.title: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface

blocks.md: A single flash package is slow by itself. In Agrawal et al.'s Samsung part, reading a page takes 25 us from the cells to the on-chip register and then about 100 us to shift 4 KB across the package's 8-bit serial bus. Done back to back that is 125 us per page: 8,000 reads per second, about 32 MB/s. Writes take 100 us of transfer plus 200 us of programming: about 3,330 per second. The trick is overlap.

blocks.title: Interleaving two dies behind one serial bus

scenes.caption: One die, no overlap: read 25 us, transfer 100 us, repeat. Three pages finish at 125, 250 and 375 us.

Two dies share the bus. While one page crosses the bus, the other die reads the next page into its own register. After the first 25 us the bus never idles: one page per 100 us, 10,000 reads per second.

blocks.md: A real SSD multiplies this across many packages on several channels, each running independently. That parallelism is only useful if the host keeps **many requests outstanding**. By Little's law, outstanding requests = throughput x latency. Agrawal et al.'s simulated SSD reads 4 KB in 130 us at 61,255 IO/s: 61,255 x 0.000130 is about 8 requests in flight at all times. A program that issues one synchronous read at a time gets one package's worth of speed.

The old Linux block layer had a single request queue protected by a single lock, which stopped scaling once devices could do hundreds of thousands of I/Os per second. **blk-mq** replaced it with per-CPU (or per-node) software staging queues feeding **hardware dispatch queues**, which map directly onto the device's own submission queues. The number of hardware queues depends on the device and driver, but is never more than the number of cores.

**NVMe** is the host interface designed for that model. Host and controller communicate through pairs of ring buffers in host memory:

- A **Submission Queue (SQ)** of 64-byte commands. A 4 KB read fits entirely in one command.
- A **Completion Queue (CQ)** of 16-byte completion entries, each carrying the command identifier, a status, the SQ head pointer, and a **phase tag** bit.

The spec allows up to 65,535 I/O queues, each with up to 65,536 slots (one slot always stays empty), plus one admin queue pair of up to 4,096 slots. Each core can own its own queue pair, so submissions need no locks.

scenes.caption: The driver writes three 64-byte commands into the next free SQ slots. These are ordinary memory stores, invisible to the device so far.
One MMIO write to the SQ tail doorbell register announces all three at once. The spec needs at most one such register write per submission.
The controller fetches the commands by DMA, executes them in any order across its flash, and DMAs the data into the host buffers.
For each finished command it writes a 16-byte entry into the CQ with the phase tag flipped, then may raise an MSI-X interrupt.
The driver reads entries from memory until the phase tag no longer matches, then writes the CQ head doorbell to hand those slots back.

blocks.md: How does the host know a CQ slot holds a *new* entry without reading a device register? The host first zeroes every phase tag. On its first pass around the ring the controller writes entries with phase tag 1; after it wraps to slot 0 it writes 0, then 1 again, and so on. The host remembers which phase it expects and stops when it sees the old value. The queue is empty when head equals tail, and full when head is one past tail, so a 6-slot queue holds at most 5 entries.

blocks.title: Phase tags in a 6-slot completion queue (NVMe spec example)

scenes.caption: Time 0: the host clears every phase tag to 0 and creates the queue. Head = tail = 0: empty.
Time 1: one command completes. The controller writes slot 0 with phase 1 and advances its internal tail to 1. The host sees 1 where it expected 1: a new entry.
Time 2: 6 completions in total fill slots 0 to 5 with phase 1; the tail wraps to 0. The host has consumed 2, so head = 2.
Time 3: completion 7 lands in slot 0 after the wrap, so its phase tag is now 0. Tail = 1, head = 2: head is one past tail, the queue is full.
Time 5: 11 completions (slots 1 to 4 now also phase 0), 8 consumed. Head = 2, tail = 5. The host is on its second pass and expects 0: slots 2 to 4 are new, slot 5 still shows 1, so it stops there.
Time 6: the host has consumed all 11. Head = tail = 5: empty. Slot 5 still shows phase 1, which the host now treats as old, since it expects 0 on this pass.

blocks.caption: Completion loop following the CQE layout: DW3 bits 15:0 command id, bit 16 phase tag, bits 31:17 status. One doorbell write covers the whole batch.

blocks.md: This design is why user-space drivers like **SPDK** can poll: checking for completions is a read of host memory for a flipped bit, with no MMIO read. SPDK gives each thread its own queue pair, so threads submit in parallel without locks, while kernel drivers usually map hardware queues to cores as close to 1:1 as possible.

NVMe queue depth does not make flash faster; it lets the controller keep many dies busy. One synchronous 4 KB read at a time pays the full read latency per request no matter how many queues the drive has. Use async I/O (io_uring, SPDK, or many threads) to keep enough requests in flight.

blocks.question: An NVMe I/O completion queue was created with 256 slots. What is the maximum number of completion entries it can hold before the controller must stop posting?
blocks.explain: The queue is full when head equals tail plus one, so one slot is always unused: 256 - 1 = 255. The spec says so explicitly: one slot in each queue is not available due to the head and tail pointer definition.

blocks.question: A host driver reaps completions by checking the phase tag. After the CQ wraps from the last slot back to slot 0, what must the driver do?
options: Nothing: new entries always have phase tag 1
Reset every phase tag in the queue to 0
Read the controller's CQ tail register
Flip the phase value it expects, because the controller now writes the opposite bit
blocks.explain: On each wrap the controller inverts the phase tag it writes. The host tracks the expected value and flips it when its head wraps. The CQ tail is internal to the controller and not visible to the host.

blocks.question: A drive delivers 500,000 random 4 KB reads per second at 100 us average latency. How many reads must the application keep outstanding to reach that rate?
blocks.explain: Little's law: outstanding = throughput x latency = 500,000 x 0.0001 s = 50. With fewer in flight, the drive's dies sit idle and throughput drops in proportion.
